figures.caption: Figure 1: Conceptual rendering of the Korean Space Telescope (KST) in its operational orbit. The spacecraft design leverages the high-resolution imaging and orbital stability heritage of the Korean Multi-Purpose Satellite (KOMPSAT) series (Lee et al., 2021b; Seo et al., 2020) to support a 1.4-meter wide-field astronomical surveyor.

Figure 2: Aperture optimization for the imaging channel. The survey grasp (etendue $\propto D^{-1}$; grey dashed) decreases with aperture, while the density of cleanly resolved and deblended galaxies in the visible (VIS) imaging channel (blue) increases as the PSF shrinks below the faint-galaxy size and then saturates. Their product, the rate at which science-usable galaxies are surveyed (red), has a genuine interior optimum at $D\approx 1.4$ m: the aperture whose $\sim 0.15^{\prime\prime}$ visible PSF matches the $\theta_{g}\sim 0.15^{\prime\prime}$ scale that must be resolved for faint-galaxy shape measurement and deblending. Below this the PSF blends the faint population and degrades shapes; above it, survey grasp is spent resolving already-resolved sources. Curves are peak-normalized; the construction is an illustrative design rationale, with the model and its inputs given in Section 2. The near-infrared channel provides $R\sim 100$ spectrophotometry (photometric redshifts and SEDs), not imaging, and is not what sets the imaging optimum.

F$i$$g$u$r$e 3: Schematic of the KST dichroic beam splitter and detector mosaics. The common incident beam is separated into simultaneous VIS and NIR channels. (a) Four CMOS detectors form a $4\times 1$ mosaic, with one fixed g, r, i, or $z$ filter per detector. (b) Twenty-seven square H2RG detectors form a $9\times 3$ mosaic beneath an LVF whose transmission wavelength varies continuously from 1.1 to 1.8 $\mu$m along the scan direction, providing $R\approx 100$ spectral mapping. Green outlines mark the identical $1^{\circ}\times 0.25^{\circ}$ science fields; hatched regions indicate detector area outside the adopted field. Both mosaics are drawn on a common scale using the 19 m effective focal length and the specified pixel pitches. Detector gaps and H2RG reference-pixel borders are omitted. Beam routing and channel orientation are schematic, and relay optics are not shown.

Figure 4: Illustrative comparison of spatial sampling in KST and SPHEREx spectral cubes. The unobscured front planes show the same illustrative galaxy with fine and coarse sampling, while the offset planes and arrows indicate the wavelength dimension. The labels give the nominal detector pixel scales: $0.195^{\prime\prime}$/pixel for KST’s NIR channel and $6.2^{\prime\prime}$/pixel for SPHEREx. Colors distinguish schematic wavelength slices, with the same underlying morphology used throughout each stack. The images provide a qualitative comparison of spatial sampling; they do not incorporate instrument-specific PSF convolution, noise, or wavelength-dependent galaxy morphology.

Figure 5: KST sensitivity. (a) $5\sigma$ limiting AB magnitude versus wavelength for a 1-hr exposure. Filled circles show KST point-source depths in $g,r,i,z$ from a first-principles exposure-time calculator (ETC) calibrated to reproduce the tabulated depths (Table 1); open circles show the corresponding $0.3^{\prime\prime}$-galaxy depths. The orange bar marks the NIR LVF per-resolution-element ($R\sim 100$) continuum depth across $1.1$–$1.8~\mu$m, which is naturally shallower than broadband imaging. Grey squares show the Euclid Wide survey for comparison (filled: point source; open: extended VIS). (b) Point-source $5\sigma$ depth versus integration time for the four VIS bands; the dotted line and filled points mark the 1-hr survey depth. The ETC assumes a 1.4-m aperture with central obscuration, CDS read noise $<5\,e^{-}$, dark current, and a conservative zodiacal$+$Earthshine sky model (bounding the low-Earth-orbit case); the effective per-band throughput is calibrated to the point-source depths of Table 1.

Figure 6: Spectroscopy without external follow-up. Schematic kilonova light curve illustrating the finite spectroscopic window (green band: the source is brighter than the spectroscopic limit, dashed line). The survey detects the transient near peak (green point), and its $R\sim 100$ spectrum accumulates during the same KST scan (blue circle). An externally triggered spectrum (orange) arrives only after trigger, scheduling, and weather latencies of days, by which time the kilonova has faded far below the spectroscopic limit and the opportunity is lost. The brightness scale is schematic.

Figure 7: LVF dispersion orientation. Two alternative design orientations, fixed at integration, for the LVF’s wavelength gradient on the $1^{\circ}\times 0.25^{\circ}$ focal plane (color shows the $1.1$–$1.8~\mu$m mapping; white lines, the $9\times 3$ NIR detector mosaic; arrow, the scan direction). (a) Dispersing along the long axis (baseline) gives a gentle gradient and keeps the vignetted edges in the cross-scan direction, at the cost of a long scan to complete each spectrum. (b) Dispersing along the short axis completes a spectrum in a $4\times$ shorter scan and crosses fewer detector gaps, but steepens the gradient and places the vignetted edges on the extreme wavelength channels.

Figure 8: Time-delay $H_{0}$ from cluster-lensed supernovae. Projected fractional precision on $H_{0}$ versus the number of multiply imaged SNe Ia with measured time delays, adopting the per-system precision of $1$–$2\%$ enabled by the standard-candle breaking of the mass-sheet degeneracy (shaded band), with an illustrative $0.4\%$ systematic floor added in quadrature; the dotted curve shows the purely statistical $2\%/\sqrt{N}$ scaling. Horizontal lines mark current published precisions: the six-system lensed-quasar measurement (Wong et al., 2020), the SH0ES distance ladder (Riess et al., 2022), and the Planck CMB inference (Planck Collaboration, 2020). At the benchmark sample of 20 systems (vertical line), KST reaches $\sigma(H_{0})/H_{0}\approx 0.5$–$0.6\%$, a sub-percent, distance-ladder-independent measurement sufficient to adjudicate the Hubble tension.

Figure 9: The error budget, not the statistics, sets the constraint. Forecast $68\%$ confidence contours in the $w_{0}$–$w_{a}$ plane for the same KST survey under three error budgets, from the systematics-marginalized Fisher analysis described in the text: statistical precision only (blue); the KST error budget, with its internally measured shear calibration, mean-redshift, and NIR supernova systematics (red); and an otherwise identical survey carrying a conventional broadband systematics chain (orange dashed). Contours are centred on the $\Lambda$CDM fiducial (star); the prior widths defining the two chains are stated in the text. Marginalizing over systematics costs the conventional chain a factor $\sim$3 in figure of merit relative to KST’s. The KST-error-budget contour corresponds to $\sigma(w_{0})=0.096$, $\sigma(w_{a})=0.36$, FoM $=79$ ($\sigma(w_{p})\approx 0.035$ at the pivot), computed for the current survey ($5{,}000$ SNe to $z\approx 1$, $n_{\rm eff}=57$, $(1+z)$-scaled redshift-bias priors); the bridge to the full-probe headline forecasts is given in the text.

Figure 10: The double-radio-relic constraint on dark-matter self-interactions. Posterior probability density of the self-interaction cross-section $\sigma/m$ from eleven merging clusters hosting symmetric double radio relics (thin curves), and their stacked constraint (thick curves; the smoothed stack in orange). The dashed and dash-dotted lines mark the resulting upper limits, $\sigma/m<0.22~\mathrm{cm^{2}\,g^{-1}}$ ($68\%$) and $<0.63~\mathrm{cm^{2}\,g^{-1}}$ ($95\%$), at the $\sim$1000–2000 km s-1 collision velocities characteristic of clusters. KST’s diffraction-limited lensing will extend this method from eleven systems to the $\gtrsim$1000 merging clusters of the Deep and Wide Surveys, projecting to $\sigma/m\lesssim 0.02~\mathrm{cm^{2}\,g^{-1}}$. Adapted from Jee et al. (2026).

2610.39094.abstract: The Korean Space Telescope (KST) is a next-generation 1.4-meter wide-field space observatory, a dedicated probe of the dark sector. Its single instrument provides diffraction-limited visible imaging (~0.15 arcsec in the optical) together with simultaneous near-infrared (R ~ 100) slitless spectrophotometry, so that every detected source is observed in the NIR by the survey itself, with spectral information delivered at a resolution set by its brightness (full R ~ 100 typing at the bright end, synthetic medium-band or broadband photometry below it) and with no separate follow-up, a capability decisive for time-domain science. With it, KST addresses the three outstanding questions of dark physics in concert: the dynamics of dark energy, the nature of dark matter, and gravitational-wave dark sirens as independent cosmological rulers. KST combines measurements of expansion and structure growth to test dark-energy models. A two-tiered "Wedding Cake" strategy (2,000 deg^2 Wide plus 10 deg^2 cluster-targeted Deep Survey) combines weak lensing, baryon acoustic oscillations, and a near-infrared-standardized Type Ia supernova Hubble diagram to constrain dark energy at its pivot redshift (sigma(w_p) ~ 0.03); maps dark matter from cluster cores to galactic substructure to test cold dark matter against warm and self-interacting alternatives; and builds a deep near-infrared host catalog for a distance-ladder-independent H_0 from dark sirens. The same data yield a Legacy Science portfolio (galaxy evolution, active galactic nuclei, exoplanets, and the Milky Way) at no additional observing cost. As Korea's first dedicated astrophysics space mission, KST occupies a niche complementary to the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, Euclid, and Roman.

2610.39881.abstract: `Adding colour'' to the gravitational-wave sky by probing unexplored frequency bands has the potential to unveil new and unexpected phenomena in the Universe. The microhertz band, between pulsar timing arrays and LISA, is a particularly attractive target: it should host the extension of the signal recently found by pulsar timing arrays (if it is generated by a family of sources of gravitational waves), and it may harbour signals from the early Universe, primordial black holes or dark matter. In these proceedings, we review how the orbits of gravitationally bound systems act as resonant detectors of microhertz gravitational waves and ultra-light dark matter. We then describe GUEST (Gravitational Universe Exploration with Satellite Tracking), a mission concept recently proposed to the ESA F-class call, consisting of two dense passive spheres covered with retroreflectors, placed in highly eccentric Earth orbits and tracked by a global laser-ranging network.

2610.39987.title: Channelled versus Isotropic Accretion of Galaxy Groups onto Clusters: Kinematics, Spin Alignment, and Assembly Bias

figures.caption: Figure 1: Geometric illustration of the distance metrics and Morse-theoretic topology used for group classification. The primary filament (order-1) connects the cluster maximum to a 2-saddle critical point; a secondary filament (order-2) connects a separate density peak (maximum) to the same 2-saddle. In Morse theory, exactly two filaments meet at each 2-saddle, each originating from a different maximum, and the material beyond the 2-saddle is conventionally assigned to the other maximum. We treat the secondary filament as connected to the cluster only because of the infall-region setting (Section 1): the probed volume lies entirely within the cluster’s gravitational sphere of influence, the cluster node is far more massive than the secondary maximum (this is not a cluster–saddle–cluster configuration), and the bulk flow is toward the cluster (Section 3.4.1). The ‘primary’/‘secondary’ labels therefore indicate each filament’s topological relationship to the cluster (Section 3.2), not an intrinsic hierarchy. Symbols are defined in Table 2.

Figure 2: Schematic of the spin-filament alignment geometry for an infalling group (symbols defined in Table 2). Because $\hat{f}$ and $\hat{r}$ are approximately co-planar (primary filaments inclined at $\approx 15^{\circ}$), the orbital angular momentum $\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{orb}}=(\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{gr}}-\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{cl}})\times(\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{gr}}-\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{cl}})\propto\hat{r}\times\hat{f}$ lies perpendicular to the filament axis, making the $\mathbf{J}$-vs-$\hat{f}$ and $\mathbf{J}$-vs-$\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{orb}}$ signals geometric complements.

Figure 3: The $XY$ projection of a massive cluster ($M_{\mathrm{vir}}=2.3\times 10^{15}\,h^{-1}\,M_{\odot}$, $\kappa=6$), showing the analysed infall sample (dominant-cluster, non-backsplash pairs) within a $\pm 10\,h^{-1}$ Mpc slab in projected depth. Dark blue filaments and points: primary (order-1) filament network and primary connected groups. Green filaments and points: secondary (order-2) network and secondary connected groups. Orange points: primary-outskirt (intermediate) groups ($1\leq d_{\mathrm{conn}}\leq 3\,h^{-1}$ Mpc). Red points: isotropic groups. Faint blue-grey lines: the post-processed $\mathrm{DisPerSE}$  filament catalogue (after the five-step cleaning of Section 2.2), with this cluster’s own order-1 and order-2 filaments drawn in colour instead. The dashed circle marks $1.5\,R_{200}$ (the connectivity shell); the dotted circle marks $7\,R_{200}$ (the outer infall/analysis boundary). Background: local halo number density.

Figure 4: Stacked transverse dark matter density profiles of MDPL2 filaments ($n_{\sigma}=6.5$, $2048^{3}$ CIC grid). (a) Model comparison for short filaments ($L_{\mathrm{fil}}=3$–$6\,h^{-1}$ Mpc), where model disparity is largest. The generalised $\beta$-model (orange) is preferred by BIC over all alternatives. Data points with error bars show azimuthally averaged stacked profiles (2000 filaments). (b) Generalised $\beta$-model fits for four filament-length bins. Dotted vertical lines mark $R_{\mathrm{c}}$ for each bin; the dashed black line at $r_{\perp}=1\,h^{-1}$ Mpc marks the $d_{\mathrm{conn}}$ classification threshold. $R_{\mathrm{c}}$ is stable at $0.54$–$0.65\,h^{-1}$ Mpc across all lengths.

Figure 5: Kinematic properties of infalling groups by accretion class (primary channelled: dark blue; secondary channelled: green; isotropic: red). Shaded bands: $\pm 1\sigma$ bootstrap uncertainties. (a) Median radial velocity $v_{r}$ vs cluster-centric distance $d_{\mathrm{cl}}/R_{200}$; negative values indicate infall. (b) Probability density of the velocity-filament angle $\theta_{\mathrm{fil}}$ (measured to the nearest filament of any type); dashed grey curve: isotropic expectation $p\propto\sin\theta$.

Figure 6: Radial profiles of alignment properties for infalling groups (colour scheme as in Fig. 5). (a) Fraction of groups with $\theta_{vf}<60^{\circ}$ (aligned within $60^{\circ}$ of the connected filament axis) vs $d_{\mathrm{cl}}/R_{200}$; dashed line: isotropic expectation (50 per cent). (b) Median velocity-filament angle $\theta_{vf}$ (solid) and velocity-radial angle $\theta_{vr}$ (dashed) for primary channelled groups; dotted lines show $\theta_{vf}$ for secondary and isotropic. The shaded band shows the near-constant $\theta_{vf}-\theta_{vr}\approx 2$–$4^{\circ}$ gap for primary groups.

Figure 7: Direct measurement of filament segment inclination angles, stacked over all $$2$6{,}6$1$6$ clusters with connected filaments. Primary filaments: dark blue circles. Secondary filaments: green squares. Dashed grey lines: isotropic expectation. (a) Median inclination angle $\varphi_{\mathrm{seg}}$ vs $d_{\mathrm{cl}}/R_{200}$; purple diamonds show the median velocity-radial angle $\theta_{vr}$ of primary groups from Fig. 6b. Figure 8: Fraction of group-cluster pairs classified as primary (dark blue), secondary (green), and isotropic (red) as a function of group virial mass. The rising channelled fractions and falling isotropic fraction reflect assembly bias: massive groups preferentially form along cluster-feeding filaments.

(b) Interpolated $M_{\mathrm{flip}}$ vs $d_{\mathrm{cl}}/R_{200}$ for primary (dark blue), secondary (green), and isotropic (red); both channelled classes flip at similar mass at all radii. (c) S along the filament spine (arc-length fraction s; $0=$ cluster, $1=$ saddle) for primary groups in two mass bins, showing the expected cTTT tidal gradient within bootstrap uncertainties. (d) $M_{\mathrm{flip}}$ vs median filament arc-length per class.

2610.39987.abstract: Galaxy clusters grow by accreting groups from the cosmic web, but whether the route of infall (along a cluster-connected filament or from the open field) imprints a group's kinematics, spin, and orbit remains unmeasured at scale. We classify $212{,}704$ group-cluster infall pairs across $27{,}029$ clusters in the $(1\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Gpc})^3$ MDPL2 simulation into primary (cluster-connected), secondary (tributary), primary-outskirt, and isotropic channels using DisPerSE filaments. (i) In both channelled classes, group spin axes lie mainly parallel to the filament below a `spin-flip' mass and perpendicular above it, $\log_{10} M_\mathrm{flip}\;[h^{-1}\,M_{\odot}] = 13.07$ and $13.12$, a $0.05$-dex offset consistent with zero, lying $1.3-1.4$ dex above the field, while isotropic groups show no flip; $M_\mathrm{flip}$ stays radially flat out to $7\,R_{200}$. (ii) Within the primary class $M_\mathrm{flip}$ rises with the linear mass density of the host filament, from $12.96$ (thin tendrils) to $13.44$ (dense bridges); matching group mass, cluster mass and distance keeps the rise positive but leaves its size uncertain ($0.07-0.58$ dex). (iii) Isotropic groups fall below random alignment at $2\,R_{200}$ ($41$ per cent within $60^\circ$, a $4.3\sigma$ deficit). Primary groups show $85$ per cent velocity-filament alignment at $2\,R_{200}$, and isotropic groups infall $150-180\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ faster, and more radially, out to $5\,R_{200}$. At matched distance isotropic groups are therefore predicted to reach orbital pericentres up to $10$ per cent smaller than primary groups, whose smaller pooled pericentres reflect only their proximity to the cluster. The topological route of accretion, and within it the host filament's linear density, shapes how groups enter clusters, testable with wide-area spectroscopic surveys.

2610.40167.title: Beyond $χ^2$: Ensemble null tests for reliable scientific discovery

figures.caption:
Fig. 1: From observations to ensemble null tests.
The three rows follow the same workflow: construct a reference, describe each
observation by a set of measurements, and compare the resulting ensembles.
CMB split maps are differenced to cancel the shared sky signal, with simulated
null maps providing the reference. Gaia stellar velocities are compared with
velocities reflected in the radial direction, and CRISPR cells carrying cutting guides
with non-targeting controls. Each map, star, or cell contributes measurements
of power across angular scales, velocity components, or cellular features.
Ensemble tests compare means, covariance-weighted distances, or full joint
distributions. The latter retain structure that simpler summaries can hide.
Bespoke tests target selected signatures within each application.

Fig. 2: Complementary sensitivities of ensemble null tests.
(A–D) Two-dimensional illustrations show a cloud of
measurements shifting, expanding, concentrating into a shell, or gathering
along preferred directions (gray, null; black, transformed).
(E–H) Detection rates for analogous changes in nine dimensions.
Bold curves highlight the most sensitive tests in each example; dashed lines mark the nominal 5%
false-positive rate. Different tests excel for different departures.
PQMass remains sensitive to all four, including angular structure hidden
from the mean and radial summaries.

Upper plots show how each contaminant changes the mean null spectrum and

2610.40167.abstract: Unrecognized systematic errors can survive standard checks and undermine scientific discoveries. Null tests and experimental controls can expose these failures, but averaging measurements or reducing them to scalar statistics can hide important structure. We propose ensemble null tests that compare multivariate distributions with references from observations or simulations. We demonstrate their benefits across science. In cosmic microwave background simulations, they detect systematic effects missed by conventional $\chi^2$ tests. In Gaia data, they detect velocity asymmetry as sensitively as an informed search. In a CRISPR screen, they expose a control mismatch in DNA damage and reveal which cellular profiles drive it. As scientific datasets grow, ensemble testing turns repeated measurements into a broader search for unknown unknowns, strengthening the empirical foundation for scientific discovery.

2610.40218.title: Celia: Catalog Embeddings Learned from cosmologIcal simulAtions

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the method. (a) The encoder tokenizes each subhalo of a catalog view from its visible input features $\boldsymbol{f}_{i}$, adds periodic spatial context from a cloud-in-cell grid and from attention biased by the separations between subhalos, and contextualizes the tokens with four induced set-attention blocks (ISAB) into the contextual states $\boldsymbol{c}_{i}$. (b) Self-supervised training on hydrodynamical catalogs of one simulation code per batch and on their N-body counterparts. The student encoder sees a masked view, in which some input groups are hidden for all subhalos (hatched columns) and the members of randomly chosen host groups keep only their positions (dark rows). It reconstructs the hidden entries and uses 32 catalog slots to predict the states $\boldsymbol{c}_{i}^{\mathrm{T}}$ that the EMA teacher assigns to the partially hidden subhalos in the complete view. Dashed paths carry no gradient. (c) After training, the frozen encoder embeds complete catalogs in blocks of at most 1,024 subhalos. The covariance of the states is vectorized and projected onto principal components of the labeled catalogs to give the catalog embedding $\boldsymbol{z}$. A linear (ridge) readout predicts the parameters from $\boldsymbol{z}$, and an error model assigns each prediction a confidence score $p_{\mathrm{conf}}$.

Figure 2: Catalog embeddings of the 600 test simulations (200 per suite), projected onto the first two principal components of the 2,100 training catalogs of IllustrisTNG, SIMBA and Astrid (equation 14). Each panel shows the same catalogs colored by one simulation parameter, and marker shapes indicate the suite. The feedback parameters are shown on logarithmic color scales, and the axis labels give the fraction of variance carried by each component.

Figure 3: Linear readout of the six simulation parameters for the 200 test catalogs of each suite (rows), using all input features. Each panel compares the prediction with the true value. The feedback parameters are shown as $\log_{10}A$. The shading gives the confidence score $p_{\mathrm{conf}}$ of each prediction (equation 19), and the numbers give the test $R^{2}$ and root-mean-square error.

Figure 4: $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$ from the 3D positions and line-of-sight velocities $v_{z}$ of galaxies with $M_{\star}>1.95\times 10^{8}\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ for the 200 test catalogs of each suite. The frozen encoder sees only these features, and a linear readout is fitted on the training catalogs. The quoted values from de Santi et al. (2023) are for their GNNs, trained and tested on their own split of the same suite. The shading gives $p_{\mathrm{conf}}$.

Figure 5: $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$ in IllustrisTNG (top) and SIMBA (bottom) from the subhalos with at least 20 star particles, using positions alone (left), positions with stellar mass, stellar half-mass radius and stellar metallicity (middle), and these with $V_{\max}$ added (right). The frozen encoder sees only these features, and a linear readout is fitted on the training catalogs. The numbers in the lower right give the test $R^{2}$ and root-mean-square error of the readout, and those in the upper left the $R^{2}$ of the GNNs of Villanueva-Domingo and Villaescusa-Navarro (2022) with the same inputs, on their own test catalogs. The shading gives $p_{\mathrm{conf}}$.

Top: zero-shot predictions of the readout fitted on the training catalogs of IllustrisTNG, SIMBA and Astrid. Bottom: predictions of a readout fitted on the 700 Swift-EAGLE training catalogs, with the shading giving $p_{\mathrm{conf}}$. The numbers give the test $R^{2}$, the root-mean-square error and, for the zero-shot predictions, the Pearson correlation r.

Lines show the median over 100 random draws of the n catalogs and bands the 16th to 84th percentiles, and $R^{2}$ below $-0.5$ is shown at $-0.5$. Figure 8: Response of the c$$a$$talog embedding to each simulation parameter (columns) in each suite (rows). For parameter a, the vertical axis is the projection $\boldsymbol{u}_{a}^{\mathsf{T}}(\boldsymbol{z}-\boldsymbol{z}_{0})$ onto the direction from the fiducial 1P catalog (diamond) to the 1P catalog with the largest value of a. Circles show the 1P catalogs and triangles the CV catalogs (Section 2.1), with the mean and standard deviation of the CV catalogs as line and gray band. Each panel gives the length $|\boldsymbol{d}|=\|\boldsymbol{d}_{a}\|$ of the displacement and the standard deviation $\sigma=\sigma_{a}$ of the CV catalogs along $\boldsymbol{u}_{a}$.

Figure 9: Statistics of the LH catalogs retrieved along straight lines in the embedding. Each panel follows one parameter in one suite (title). The line runs from the embedding of the 1P catalog with the lowest value of the parameter ($t=0$) to that of the 1P catalog with the highest value ($t=1$), and each of 11 equally spaced points on it is represented by the mean statistic of the five nearest of all 1,000 LH catalogs of the same suite. $\Phi$ is the number of subhalos per unit volume and per dex in dark-matter mass, $V_{\max}$ or stellar mass. The other panels show medians in bins of halo or stellar mass, with the stellar-to-halo mass ratio taken for central galaxies and $f_{\mathrm{b}}$ the baryon fraction of a FoF halo. Only bins populated in at least half of the training catalogs are shown. The lower part of each panel gives the ratio to the midpoint of the line, $t=0.5$.

Figure 10: Cross-fitted cosine similarity between the response directions of the six parameters in the three suites, estimated from all 1,000 LH catalogs of each suite. Red cells mark parameters that move catalogs in similar directions and blue cells opposite directions, and isotropic random directions give zero. The bottom row (IC, initial conditions) gives the root-mean-square cosine between each direction and the displacements between pairs of CV catalogs of the same suite. The mark on the color bar shows its value for isotropic random directions.

2610.40218.abstract: Cosmological hydrodynamical simulations connect observed galaxies to cosmology and the physics of galaxy formation. Each simulation is expensive, and different codes model galaxy formation in different ways. We present Celia (Catalog Embeddings Learned from cosmologIcal simulAtions), a self-supervised foundation model that maps catalogs of subhalos and their galaxy properties to an embedding vector for the purposes of compression and organization of astrophysical and large-scale structure information. Celia is pretrained without parameter labels on the IllustrisTNG, SIMBA and Astrid suites of CAMELS and their N-body counterparts, by reconstructing masked subhalo properties and predicting the representations of a teacher network. Simple linear models fitted to the embeddings recover $\Omega_{\mathrm m}$ with $R^2=0.999$, and $\sigma_8$ and both supernova-feedback amplitudes with $R^2\geq0.97$, in all three suites. The embeddings translate well to out-of-distribution simulations such as Swift-EAGLE, a code that Celia never saw. A linear model fitted on the three training codes predicts its $\Omega_{\mathrm m}$ with a correlation coefficient $r=0.985$, and linear models fitted on 20 labeled simulations reach $r\geq0.94$ for $\Omega_{\mathrm m}$, $\sigma_8$ and a supernova-feedback amplitude. We decompose the variation among the simulations of each suite into principal components of the embedding, and simple power laws of the simulation parameters describe the leading components. Celia gives simulated galaxy catalogs a shared coordinate system for simulation-based inference, emulation, the comparison of galaxy-formation models, the detection of physical degeneracies and the discovery of new astrophysical probes.

2610.40610.abstract: At high redshift, the cosmic microwave background (CMB) both cools relativistic leptons and provides seed photons for inverse-Compton (IC) X-ray emission. These two effects link the particle content of a bubble directly to the soft X-ray depression used to identify a cavity. We derive a physical criterion connecting lepton cooling, bubble volume, enthalpy evolution, and 0.5--2 keV X-ray visibility, while separating intrinsic filling of the X-ray depression from detector-dependent cavity recovery. For uncooled electron populations described by a power law with spectral index $s=2.5$, minimum Lorentz factor $100\leq\gamma_{\min}\leq1000$, and maximum Lorentz factor $\gamma_{\max}=10^5$, the measured atmosphere of the testbed high-redshift cluster SPT-CL J2215$-$3537 requires 0.6--1.2\% of the pressure in radiating leptons to fill the soft-band deficit. Across the full tested ranges of $s$, $\gamma_{\min}$, and atmospheric properties, the required fraction is 0.2--3.7\%. Complete loss of this component reduces the enthalpy by less than 3\% relative to an otherwise identical adiabatic bubble at the same pressure. A low-cutoff control with $\gamma_{\min}=10$ and $s=3$ instead requires 18.9\%, identifying the poorly constrained low-energy spectrum as the main physical uncertainty. For a fixed atmosphere and spectrum, the required fraction scales as $(1+z)^{-4}$. The declining-pressure tracks show that the X-ray deficit can cross the adopted detection threshold while the enthalpy deficit remains below 0.4\%; the time of this transition depends on the assumed pressure history. Thus, high-redshift cavity visibility depends on both the surrounding atmosphere and the pressure-carrying particle spectrum. This criterion provides the physical basis for an instrument-specific recovery analysis.
